title: Derivatives and Gradients
scope: Understand local rate of change as the signal that tells a learning system which direction changes an output.
beginnerEntry: You can read function graphs, slope, and changes in numeric values.

knowledge.history: Newton and Leibniz independently invented calculus in the 1660s-80s to capture instantaneous change — the speed of a planet at a moment, not over an hour. That same 'slope right here, right now' is the gradient that tells a neural network which way to adjust every weight.

mentalModels.name: Speedometer, not odometer
mentalModels.description: The odometer tells you total distance; the speedometer tells you the rate right now. A derivative is the speedometer of any changing quantity.

mentalModels.name: Zoom until it looks straight
mentalModels.description: Zoom far enough into any smooth curve and it becomes indistinguishable from a straight line. The slope of that line is the derivative at that point.

analogies.analogy: A car speedometer reading at one instant of a journey
analogies.whenToUse: When separating instantaneous rate from accumulated total.

analogies.analogy: Feeling the steepness of a hiking trail underfoot at each step
analogies.whenToUse: When introducing slope as a local, position-dependent quantity.

objectives: Explain average and local rate of change.
Estimate a derivative from nearby values.
Differentiate simple linear and quadratic functions intuitively.
Interpret a gradient as multi-parameter sensitivity.

steps.prompt: A car travels 10 km in the first hour and 30 km in the next. Compare average speed over two hours with speed at a particular instant.
How can increasingly small input steps reveal the slope of a curved function at one point?
For y = x squared, compare output changes near x = 1 and x = 4. Predict where the graph is steeper and the sign of each slope.
Play the slope experiment above: slide from x = -3 to x = 3. Where is the slope steepest, where is it zero, and what is special about the point where it is zero?
Break it: try to state 'the slope of the curve' as one single number for the whole curve. Why is that impossible, and what does that force the derivative to be?
State your discovery: the derivative is itself a function — a rule (2x) giving the instantaneous slope at every point — and the sign of that slope tells you which direction is downhill.
A derivative is local output change per input change. A gradient collects one derivative per input or parameter, pointing toward fastest increase.

Your speedometer is a derivative: distance change per time change, right now. Name two more everyday derivatives, such as a heating bill's sensitivity to thermostat setting or weight change per week, and state each one's input, output, and sign.

A bakery's daily profit depends on two dials: price and batch size. Nudging price up 10 cents changes profit by one amount; baking one extra batch changes it by another. Two sensitivities, one system.

If you could only measure how profit responds to tiny nudges of each dial, never see the whole profit curve, could you still climb toward the best settings? Which dial should you turn first, and in which direction?
Profit sensitivity is +3 per unit of price and -2 per unit of batch size at today's settings. Predict what happens to profit if each dial is nudged up slightly, and which single change helps most.

That pair of sensitivities, (+3, -2), is a gradient. A learning system treats its parameters as dials, measures the gradient of its objective, and nudges every parameter in the direction that improves the outcome. This is the engine inside model training.

Estimate the derivative of x squared at x = 3 using values at 2.99 and 3.01, and interpret the sign for an optimizer. Notice the limitation: knowing which way is downhill is useless until something says what counts as downhill. Learning needs a score to minimize: the loss.

experiments.title: Ride the tangent line
experiments.instructions: Slide a point along the curve y = x² and watch the tangent line tilt. The slope readout is 2x — the derivative, changing from point to point.

measurement.prePrompt: Explain slope and how you might measure the steepness of a curve at one point.
measurement.postPrompt: Estimate a local derivative numerically, interpret its sign and magnitude, and explain how a two-component gradient describes sensitivity to two parameters.

checks.label: Describe a rate of change or slope.
Use the sign or direction of the slope.
Reference the derivative or gradient explicitly.
Connect derivatives to optimization or learning.

misconceptions: A derivative is the function value.
A positive derivative means the output is positive.
A gradient directly gives the best parameter values.
reasoning.tutorGuidance: Return to rise over run, shrink the run around one point, and ask what sign and size say about a small parameter increase. Separate current value from current slope.
